title: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA tutorial showing how two GB300-based DGX Stations linked over ConnectX-8 RDMA can serve the 753B-parameter GLM-5.3 NVFP4 MoE model (~464 GB, too big for one 252 GB GPU) via vLLM tensor parallelism behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. AIPerf on SPEED-Bench Coding shows throughput peaking at 607.8 tok/s at concurrency 16 and degrading at 32, pitching desk-side frontier-scale inference for private data and no per-token costs.

themes.theme: Frontier models outgrow a single GPU

insights.claim: Frontier-scale models no longer fit in the memory of a single machine, so running them locally with all weights in GPU memory now requires spanning multiple machines.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Local/edge inference demand pushes buyers toward multi-node workstation purchases and high-speed interconnect, expanding NVIDIA's attach rate.
insights.quote: the largest models no longer fit on one machine

insights.claim: NVIDIA's GLM-5.3 NVFP4, a quantized version of Z.ai's mixture-of-experts model, has 753 billion parameters with 40 billion activated per token, and its checkpoint is about 464 GB.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is packaging third-party Chinese open-weight models in its own NVFP4 format, tying model distribution to Blackwell-class hardware.

insights.claim: Sparse MoE activation reduces compute per token but does not reduce memory needs, because every expert's weights must stay resident since each token can be routed to different experts.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: MoE architectures shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to memory capacity, favoring high-HBM products and memory suppliers.
insights.quote: Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available

insights.claim: The ~464 GB GLM-5.3 NVFP4 checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU, so the tutorial uses two DGX Stations with CPU weight offload disabled.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Per-GPU HBM capacity is the gating spec for local frontier inference; capacity gaps translate directly into multi-unit sales.

insights.claim: NVFP4 quantization in the GLM-5.3 checkpoint targets only MoE-block linear weights and activations rather than every tensor, which is why the config reports MIXED_PRECISION.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Selective FP4 quantization is how NVIDIA shrinks frontier models onto its hardware without full-model precision loss.
insights.quote: NVFP4 quantization targets MoE-block linear weights and activations, not every tensor

insights.claim: With tensor parallelism (TP=2) across two DGX Stations, each GB300 holds and computes roughly half the weights (about 218 GiB per GPU), and every token requires both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Cross-node inference makes the network fabric (ConnectX-8 RDMA) a first-class part of the product, not an add-on.
insights.quote: every token needs both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail
insights.locator: At this point one model spans two machines

insights.claim: After loading GLM-5.3, each Station's GB300 used about 231.3 GiB of GPU memory including weights, KV cache and runtime buffers, versus near zero before loading.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Model nearly saturates available HBM, leaving limited headroom for KV cache and concurrency.
insights.locator: Table 1. GPU memory before and after

insights.claim: The two Stations are linked by direct ConnectX-8 rails with an expected 400000Mb/s link and MTU 9000, and communication must run over GPU RDMA rather than falling back to TCP sockets.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Shows NVIDIA networking (ex-Mellanox) bundled into workstation-class AI, broadening networking revenue beyond data centers.
insights.locator: These checks catch cabling and addressing mistakes

insights.claim: The tutorial pins NCCL 2.30.7 from the vLLM image because older versions can deadlock cross-node CUDA graph replays over RoCE.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Multi-node local inference still has software fragility; maturity of the stack is a gating factor for adoption.

themes.theme: Serving optimizations: MTP, FP8 KV cache, prefix caching

insights.claim: vLLM is configured with multi-token prediction, a form of speculative decoding in which the model's MTP layer drafts four tokens per step that the full model verifies, with gains depending on how often drafts are accepted.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Speculative decoding is a software lever for raising tokens per GPU, improving the economics of owned hardware.

insights.claim: Storing the KV cache in FP8 halves cache memory compared with 16-bit storage, leaving room for more tokens in flight, while prefix caching avoids reprocessing previously seen prompt prefixes.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Memory-saving techniques directly expand concurrency on fixed hardware.
insights.quote: FP8 KV-cache storage halves cache memory compared with 16-bit storage
insights.locator: FP8 KV-cache storage halves cache memory

insights.claim: The KV cache occupies the GPU memory left after weights and is shared by all in-flight requests, so longer prompts or more users require more of it, and operators must lower max context length or concurrency when it runs out.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Memory headroom, not compute, caps how many users a local deployment can serve.
insights.locator: The remaining GPU memory holds the KV cache

themes.theme: Benchmark results and the concurrency trade-off

insights.claim: On SPEED-Bench Coding with prefix caching, four MTP draft tokens and FP8 KV cache, overall output throughput on two DGX Stations was 107.4 tok/s at concurrency 1, 386.0 at C8, peaked at 607.8 at C16, and fell to 385.0 at C32.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete capacity ceiling (~600 tok/s) for a two-workstation frontier-model setup, useful for sizing local-AI TAM versus cloud.

insights.claim: Mean request latency rose from 49.84 s at concurrency 1 to 453.54 s at concurrency 32, and mean per-user throughput dropped from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Two-node local serving suits a handful of users or agents, not broad multi-tenant workloads, limiting its substitution of cloud endpoints.
insights.quote: Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32.

insights.claim: Mean time-to-first-token stayed around 434-483 ms from concurrency 1 to 16 but jumped to 4899.36 ms at concurrency 32, while mean inter-token latency rose from 8.78 to 77.90 ms/token.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Shows a sharp saturation knee past 16 concurrent requests, consistent with the configured max-num-seqs limits.

insights.claim: NVIDIA positions a desk-side two-Station deployment of a 753B-parameter model as enabling inference on sensitive or proprietary data, local agent prototyping, and prompt iteration without per-token costs.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Signals NVIDIA's push to sell high-end local AI hardware as an alternative to hosted APIs, a potential competitive pressure on per-token cloud pricing.
insights.quote: running inference on sensitive or proprietary data, prototyping agents locally, and iterating on prompts without per-token costs

insights.claim: Because the vLLM launcher enables tool calling, agent frameworks using the OpenAI tools API can call the same local GLM-5.3 endpoint.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: OpenAI API compatibility lowers switching costs from hosted models to open-weight local deployments.

insights.claim: The tutorial warns that the default launch exposes an unauthenticated API on every Station A interface, requiring firewalling, authentication and TLS before wider access.
insights.speaker: Fatima Fall
insights.so_what: Enterprise-grade security still falls on the operator for local AI stacks.
